opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, there are really two layers to the problem.

The first is credit assignment. When an agent runs a long, multi-step task, like navigating a codebase, filling out a web form, or chaining tool calls, the failure you observe at the end often isn't caused by the last step. Something went subtly wrong five or ten steps earlier: a wrong assumption, a misread observation, an API call that returned something unexpected that the model just glossed over. So the agent has to look back over its own trajectory and work out where things actually diverged. That's hard, because the signal is sparse and delayed, and models are often overconfident about their intermediate reasoning.

The second layer is what you do once you've found the failure. Within a single episode, you want the agent to recover. It should notice an error message or an unexpected state, reflect on it, and try a different strategy rather than repeating the same action in a loop, which is a surprisingly common failure mode. Across episodes, you want the lesson to persist. That could be in-context, by carrying forward a summary of what went wrong. It could be through some form of memory. Ultimately it could be through training, where those failed trajectories become data. Failures are actually very informative training signal if you can label them well. A trajectory that almost worked, plus a note on where it broke, can teach the model more than another clean success.

What makes this especially tricky is that pretraining data is mostly finished artifacts. It's polished code and final answers, not the messy process of trying something, seeing it fail, and backing up. So models haven't seen much of that recovery behavior. A lot of the current work, both in post-training with reinforcement learning on agentic environments and in how we design the scaffolding, is about teaching models that loop: act, observe, diagnose, revise. And they need to do it efficiently, without burning through a huge number of steps or compute.

So I'd frame it as a combination of better self-evaluation, meaning knowing when you're wrong and why, and better ways of turning those mistakes into durable improvement. Both are pretty open research problems right now.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that this is really the crux of what makes agents different from a single model call. When you're doing one-shot generation, there's no notion of a step that went wrong and then having to recover from it. But when an agent is executing a multi-step task, say it's navigating a website, or writing and running code, or calling a sequence of tools, it's almost guaranteed that some of those intermediate steps will fail. The API returns an error, the code doesn't compile, the page doesn't have the element it expected. And the question becomes, what does the agent do with that signal?

And I think there are really two layers to it. The first layer is at inference time, in the moment. Can the model actually recognize that the step failed? That sounds trivial but it often isn't. A lot of failures are silent, or the error message is ambiguous, or the model is overconfident and just keeps going as if the step succeeded. So you need the model to be able to read the environment feedback, update its understanding of the state of the world, and then re-plan rather than just retrying the same thing. And we see a lot of models get stuck in these loops where they try the same action three or four times because they don't actually incorporate the feedback.

The second layer is the training question, which is, how do you get the model to be better at this over time? And this is where it gets interesting because the data you want is trajectories that include failures and recoveries. If you only train on clean, successful trajectories, which is what a lot of the supervised data looks like, the model has never seen what it looks like to hit a wall and back out. So it's actually out of distribution the moment something goes wrong. One approach is to collect or synthesize trajectories where you deliberately include the failed steps and then the correction, so the model learns that pattern. The other is reinforcement learning, where you let the agent explore, and the reward is on the final outcome, and the model has to figure out on its own that recovering from a mistake is part of getting to the reward.

The hard part with the RL framing is credit assignment. If you have a task that takes thirty steps and the agent fails at the end, which of those steps was the problem? And you often don't have a dense reward signal that tells you. So there's a lot of work on building better verifiers, or process rewards, that can score intermediate steps, and that's really where a lot of the progress has come from.

And the last thing I'd say is that the environment matters enormously. A lot of what makes failure recovery hard isn't the model, it's that the environment doesn't give good feedback. If the error message just says "something went wrong," no amount of model capability fixes that. So part of the challenge is actually designing the tools and the interfaces so that failures are legible, because that's what makes learning from them possible in the first place.

astra-6.text:
I think the key challenge is that a failed step doesn’t necessarily tell the agent what it should have done instead. It has to understand whether it chose the wrong action, made an incorrect assumption, or simply didn’t have enough information. And when a task involves many steps, the mistake may have happened well before the failure became visible.

So the agent needs a feedback loop: take an action, observe what happened, and use that observation to revise its approach. But the important question is whether that revision actually changes its behavior. Can it avoid repeating the same mistake, and can it apply what it learned when the situation is slightly different? That’s a higher bar than being able to produce a convincing explanation of why it failed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key challenge is that a failed step doesn’t necessarily tell the agent what it should have done instead. It has to understand whether it chose the wrong action, made an incorrect assumption, or simply didn’t have enough information. And sometimes that failure only becomes apparent several steps later, so figuring out which decision to learn from is difficult.

What we would like is for the agent to use that feedback to revise its approach, rather than just repeat the same action. It needs to keep track of what it tried, reason about what the outcome tells it, and explore an alternative. Then there’s a second question: can it carry that lesson into a new task? Recovering within one interaction is useful, but learning something that generalizes beyond that interaction is a much harder problem.
